name: Sheldon somatotypes

card.summary: A three-part body-type scheme (ectomorph, mesomorph, endomorph) that lifters and looksmaxxers use to describe frame, leanness and muscle-gain tendencies when planning how to build a better physique.
card.note: Sheldon's original link between body type and personality is rejected by modern researchers; sport science uses a modified method.

quick.overview:
Somatotypes are a way of sorting physiques into three poles: ectomorph (slender, linear), mesomorph (muscular, athletic) and endomorph (rounder, softer, stores fat easily). Psychologist William Sheldon introduced the scheme in the 1940s, and the words have since become everyday gym vocabulary.

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles the labels are used to set expectations and pick strategies: ectomorphs talk about eating more and training for width, endomorphs about leanness, mesomorphs about how they respond to training. Sport-science researchers still measure somatotypes in athletes with a later method, while Sheldon's claims about personality are not accepted.
quick.how: People self-type from frame cues such as wrist and ankle size, shoulder width and how easily they gain muscle or fat, and then tailor calories, training volume and exercise selection. Researchers instead use the Heath-Carter method, which combines skinfolds, girths, bone breadths, height and weight into three numeric scores.
quick.risks: No physical risk attaches to the labels themselves. The main caveat reported by critics is that the categories are loose and that treating them as fixed ceilings can shape expectations; some forum users also cite them when justifying steroid use.

lead: Sheldon somatotypes are a classification of human physique into three components named ectomorphy, mesomorphy and endomorphy, proposed by the American psychologist William Herbert Sheldon in the 1940s.[1] In gym and looksmaxxing language the terms describe a person's natural build: ectomorphs are slim and linear and find it hard to add weight, mesomorphs are muscular with a narrow waist, and endomorphs are softer and find it harder to get lean.[1]

People use the labels to plan how to improve their physique. Lifters who call themselves ectomorphs discuss training choices suited to long limbs, eating in a surplus, and the way shoulders and frame shape the finished look,[2][3] while endomorph and mesomorph labels are used in debates about diet and responsiveness to training.[4] On looksmax.org, ectomorph threads concern how big a naturally lean frame can get and how it looks at different levels of muscle.[2]

Sheldon developed the system in The Varieties of Human Physique (1940) and the Atlas of Men (1954), rating each component from 1 to 7 and linking each type to temperament.[1] Researchers later replaced his photographic method with the Heath-Carter anthropometric method, which is still used in sport science to describe athletes in soccer, basketball, taekwondo, jiu-jitsu and other sports.[5][6][7] Sheldon's personality claims, and his data practices, have been widely criticised by scholars.[1]

chain: Match calories, training and exercise choices to the type
angle.text: Somatotype labels give lifters a shared vocabulary for their natural frame, which they use to set goals and choose training and eating approaches. Athletes' somatotypes are also measured in sport science to describe typical builds by sport.

infobox: The Varieties of Human Physique (1940); Atlas of Men (1954)

paras: Sheldon named the three components after embryonic germ layers. Endomorphy describes a rounder, softer build with a tendency to store fat; mesomorphy a muscular, strong build with a narrow waist; ectomorphy a slender, often tall build that gains weight and muscle with difficulty.[1] Each person is described by three numbers, so a pure endomorph scores 7-1-1, a pure mesomorph 1-7-1 and a pure ectomorph 1-1-7, though most people are blends.[1]

Sheldon's original ratings came from standardised photographs. The later Heath-Carter method derives the three scores from body mass, height, skinfold thicknesses, girths and bone breadths, with ectomorphy calculated from the ponderal index.[1] A modified somatotype method was published in 1967.[8]

Sheldon published The Varieties of Human Physique in 1940, The Varieties of Temperament in 1942 and the Atlas of Men in 1954, pairing each body type with a temperament.[1] Critics say the project had roots in eugenics, that its data handling would not meet current standards, and that his own assistant Barbara Honeyman Heath accused him of falsifying data.[1] The temperament claims are now widely dismissed, while the body-type framework survived in modified form.[1]

Systematic reviews report somatotype characteristics for professional soccer players,[5] taekwondo athletes (a blend of moderate musculoskeletal development and relative linearity),[6] and basketball players, where guards tend to be lighter and more mesomorphic than centres.[7] A review of soccer players found somatotype among the factors distinguishing players of different level and position.[9]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting communities
paras: Forum users use ectomorph, mesomorph and endomorph as shorthand for frame and gaining tendencies. One looksmax.org thread argues that ectomorphs with decent shoulders look most aesthetic when using anabolic steroids, while mesomorphs can look bulky.[2] Another asks for exercise substitutions for a long-armed ectomorph, such as front squats, floor presses and trap-bar deadlifts, and posters describe slow gains despite high calorie intake.[3] Contributors on T Nation sometimes describe ectomorphs as people who overstimulate and under-recover, and some say the labels cannot predict which training routine a person will respond to.[10][11]

Human studies use somatotype mainly as a descriptive measure rather than a treatment. Reviews have profiled the physiques of soccer, basketball, taekwondo and jiu-jitsu athletes,[5][6][7][12] and one randomised trial examined aquatic exercise and postural mobility in older adults with an endomorphic somatotype.[13] No trial has tested whether training or diet matched to somatotype produces better physique outcomes than unmatched approaches.

timeline.event: Sheldon publishes The Varieties of Human Physique.[1]
The Varieties of Temperament links body type to personality.[1]
Atlas of Men presents the 1-7 rating scale.[1]
A modified somatotype method is published in the American Journal of Physical Anthropology.[8]

lore.intro: Somatotype terms appear throughout lifting and looksmaxxing threads as a way to explain why people gain or lose weight differently.[2][3]

claims.claim: Ectomorphs cannot look big without steroids
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster states that ectomorphs will not look big without steroids, adding that ectomorphs with good shoulders look most aesthetic on them.[2]
claims.experts: No published study has tested this claim; somatotype research describes athletes' builds rather than natural size ceilings.[5][7]

claims.claim: Ectomorphs need specific exercise variations for their lever lengths
claims.believers: A forum user with long arms prefers front squats, floor presses and trap-bar deadlifts to suit his proportions.[3]
claims.experts: No trial has compared exercise selection by somatotype.

claims.claim: Somatotype does not predict which training works
claims.believers: A T Nation contributor says body-type information cannot determine the routine or volume a person will respond to.[10]
claims.experts: Sheldon's framework has been criticised on methodological grounds,[1] and modern somatotyping is used to describe builds.[5]
